feedback: If the child says a bigger-looking build 'has more' pieces, re-separate and re-count together; spread the pieces of the smaller build into a long line so 'looks more' is uncoupled from 'is more'.
If the child thinks pieces 'went away' with the first object, hold up the full pile and recount: the arrangement ended, but every piece is still here and could rebuild the original.
Reinforce correct reasoning: 'Yes — same pieces, same count, just arranged differently.'
Prompt for evidence, not just assertion: 'How do we KNOW the pieces are all still here?' — expect counting and one-to-one matching as the answer.
activities.intendedInsight: The object can disappear and reappear as something completely new, but not one piece is created or lost — the same small set of pieces is simply rearranged. This is evidence-based: you can count and match the pieces to prove it.
learnerActions: Take a small, countable set of pieces (e.g. 8 building bricks or magnetic tiles) and build one object, such as a robot.
Count every piece in the object, touching each one (or count them before you build), and record the number (e.g. 8). Draw or photograph the pieces so you have a record to check against later.
Take the object fully apart so the pieces are loose and scattered.
Rebuild the SAME pieces into a clearly different object, such as a car.
Count and lay out the pieces again, and compare with your first count: if no piece was dropped, lost or added, the number is the same (8).
Line up the pieces one-to-one against your first count and your drawing or photo of the original pieces to confirm it is the same set — none appeared, none vanished.
Say aloud what changed (the arrangement / the object) and what did not change (the pieces themselves and their count).
activities.title: Build, take apart, rebuild — same pieces, new object

feedback: If the child uses extra or fewer pieces for the second build, pause and recount: the challenge is to use the same set each time.
Celebrate the realisation: 'The same box of pieces made two totally different things!'
activities.intendedInsight: A single small set of pieces can make many different objects — the variety lives in the arrangement, while the set of pieces stays the same.
learnerActions: Starting from one fixed set of pieces, build two different things, one after the other (e.g. a dog, then a car), using every piece each time.
After each build, confirm the piece count is unchanged.
Describe in words or a drawing that both objects came from exactly the same pieces.
activities.title: One box, two creations challenge

feedback: If the child's example involves things that cannot simply be un-made (e.g. paints that have been mixed together, or something that has been burned), gently note that this idea is about reassembling discrete, countable parts — reusing bricks is not the same as trying to undo a paint mixture or a burn.
Affirm good connections: 'Yes — rebuilding Lego uses the same bricks in a new way, just like our build.'
activities.intendedInsight: Keeping pieces as pieces and reusing them is something people do in real life; the object changes but the material carries over.
learnerActions: Photograph or draw the same pieces in both arrangements, with the matching piece count noted for each.
Make a simple 'same pieces, new object' record sheet showing the before and after builds and the equal counts.

Name an everyday example of reusing pieces to make something new — e.g. dismantling a Lego model to build a new one, or taking apart an old toy and using its wheels and screws to build something different.
Explain why that example is the same idea: the pieces are reused, not made from scratch.
activities.title: Record and connect to real reuse

feedback: If the child gives a different count for the second object, or says pieces 'went away with' the first object, re-separate and re-count together to show the set is intact.
On the reversibility probe, affirm that because all the pieces are still here, the first object could be rebuilt exactly — which shows nothing was lost, only rearranged.

If the child answers 'where did it go?' as if the material itself disappeared, hold up the pile: the arrangement ended but the pieces are all here and could rebuild it — reconnect object versus material.
If two pieces were genuinely removed, help the child see the count really does change now — because pieces were taken away, not because rebuilding destroys pieces.
Reinforce full reasoning: 'Same pieces, same count, new arrangement — the object is an arrangement that can end while the pieces stay.'
activities.intendedInsight: The count must stay the same because it is the same pieces in a new arrangement. The first object (an arrangement) no longer exists, but every piece (the material) still does — so the original could even be rebuilt. The object ending is not the same as the material vanishing.
learnerActions: Observe an adult build an object from 10 pieces, take it apart, and build a different object from the very same pieces.
Before the rebuild is re-counted, PREDICT how many pieces the new object has and WHY.
Answer: 'Did any pieces get made or disappear — how do you know?'
Answer: 'Could you build the exact same first object again from these pieces? What does that tell us?'
Answer the deeper question: 'The first object is gone — so where did it go?'
Try the variant: imagine (or watch) two pieces slipped into a pocket before the rebuild — now what is different, and why?
activities.title: Diagnose and discuss: where did the object go?
